utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. I would like the witness/accused to come in directly and take his place at the witness bench. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, Defence and Prosecution counsel. Good morning to the accused, and let me give the floor immediately to Mr. Nobilo for a hearing that will continue until 1.30 with an approximate 15-minute break. Mr. Nobilo, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you tell the Court, in 1992, from the time you took over the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, which was called the regional main staff of the HVO to begin with, what were your basic two functions in that particular year for that territory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my two basic functions were to carry out defence along the front lines and to stand at the head of combat operations, and the second duty was the organisation of the army, that is to say, the army made up of the armed people or the armed villagers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first topic we should like to talk about today would be the front, the front lines towards the army of the Republika Srpska. We have already introduced a map showing the front, the different front lines and fronts, but could you now go through the situation month by month and tell us which fronts were active, where the fighting actually took place, and where you took place in directing and organising the defence, having taken over the command of the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Already in July 1992, the active fronts were Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Komusina, Usora, Jajce, Jablanica, and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in August, what fronts were active?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In August, the following fronts continued to be operative: Jajce, Komusina, which the Serbs had taken over on the 8th of August, 1992, and they expelled about 6.000 civilians from that area. Then there was Usora, Maglaj, Jablanica, and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about September? What were your preoccupations in September?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In September, there was Kupres, Jajce, Usora, Maglaj, Zepce, Olovo, Gorazde, Stup, and the area around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October, what fronts were active?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Usora, Jajce, Maglaj, Olovo, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, in November and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They were the areas of Novi Travnik, Travnik, Usora, Maglaj, Olovo, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the fronts that you enumerated fronts in which the HVO was confronting the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the front in Gorazde, where the HVO gave logistical assistance to all the other fronts, the HVO forces took part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you responsible for those HVO forces, that is to say, did they come under the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I've got the translation and the transcript. The witness said that the HVO was who was supporting -- I only heard "aside from" or "except for Gorazde." I didn't hear the rest of the answer. General Blaskic, aside from Gorazde, I think that you said that the HVO was fighting on all the fronts; is that correct? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, apart from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the adversaries, the enemies, were the army of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, the HVO, which engaged in defence operations on those fronts, were they under your military responsibility?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In all these areas, the answer is yes, but in October, the Operative Zone was reorganised, and Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Jablanica, and Konjic were not within the composition of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, from October 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the fronts or some regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which you either assisted or where troops were fighting, were dominantly Muslim in terms of population, particularly in eastern Bosnia. Could you explain your interest in assisting the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslim regions, in fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At all events, as soon as I took over my duties, I did everything in my power to include all potential forces at our disposal into the defence of the regions where the combat operations were taking place against the Serbs, and I was conscious of the fact that an attack on the Serbs would be selective, taking over and control step by step the entire area. So the military interest was supreme and was the primary interest in setting up our defence, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, the municipality of Gorazde and Olovo, were these predominantly Muslim municipalities in view of the ethnic composition of the population?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were predominantly Bosniak Muslim municipalities, but the representative of the supreme authority from Gorazde felt the need, and, in November, he visited the command of the Operative Zone and expressed publicly at press conferences his gratitude for the assistance given in the defence to help him defend Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "Gorazde," you mean in eastern Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you find the resources to send to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in eastern Bosnia? How did you deal with logistics?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Before the defence operations were launched, that was the most difficult question for us to solve because there was not enough logistics to ensure the functioning of the front, and this was especially true as of September. What we would do is we would take from the municipalities that were not on the front lines, such as the municipality of Vitez, for example, then there was the municipality of Busovaca, the municipality of Fojnica, and the municipality of Kresevo are cases in point, so we would take ammunition and armaments and other resources which we would then send to those areas which were subjected to the attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The greatest losses were incurred in Jajce. A large portion of the territory was taken control of by the Serbs, and 25.000 people fled to the Lasva River Valley. Can you explain what happened in Jajce? What was your involvement there at the front in Jajce, and how did you cooperate with the Territorial Defence forces, and, ultimately, what was the effect of the fall of Jajce itself?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In order to take control of Jajce, the enemy, the Serbian army, engaged almost two corps. It was the 2nd Krajina Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps. The front at Jajce was 107 kilometres long, and of that area, the HVO covered 80 kilometres, controlled 80 kilometres, whereas the Territorial Defence had about 27 kilometres. I, myself, from the 12th of August and practically the entire time after that, spent at that front commanding directly the defence operations, and we succeeded, in the course of that period, to engage from Central Bosnia about 300 volunteers per week at that front, the front of Jajce. During a lull when there were no attacks from the Serb side, I was engaged in organising the defence operations, and I tried to use specific methods by which to replace our lack in military organisation. I organised defence at Jajce in sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean when you say that you organised defence according to different sectors? Is that a modern method of warfare or is that a method of warfare that was used in past times? What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, it is not a modern method of warfare, and what it meant was that I had ten associates or up to ten assistants, and I gave them the task of controlling a certain portion of the terrain up at the front line which they were to defend, I assigned them a portion of the front to defend of the 80 kilometres that the HVO covered at the Jajce front. It was not a classical method of warfare and combat operations because, at that time in Jajce, we had armed villages, and in the aim of improving the effectiveness of our defence, I held meetings with the representatives of the Territorial Defence, I had meetings with the representatives of HOS, and I endeavoured to improve cooperation, particularly in the combat operations and putting them into effect. Our greatest problem was the imbalance that existed in weaponry and manpower between the attackers, that is to say, the Serbian army, and the defenders on the other side, and the air force was used very frequently in the area and helicopter units as well. These were used on the part of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Together with Jajce, you also had another very active front in October, and that was the Maglaj front. Could you tell us of the casualties incurred there and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In October, I spent a considerable time at that front, and it encompassed the entire area from Novi Seher, Usora, and Maglaj, and the Serbs endeavoured to take control of Maglaj, and there was intensive fighting, intense combat operations in the area. The command, of which I was the commander in chief, from June onwards, were in the area. When I was not there, my deputy commander was there. He was Luka Sekerija, and in Maglaj, there was a coordinated action, and the joint command of the defence of Maglaj worked together, and this joint command was led by Robert Bresic. He was the commander of that joint command, and his deputy was Sulejman Herceg. Within that composition, there was also Alojz Gasparevic within the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The units that defended Maglaj, what were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, in that area, we succeeded in engaging parts of HOS, then units of the Territorial Defence, as well as the Green Legion, Zelene Legija, and the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the casualties in October at that front?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that front, about 43 soldiers were killed up until the beginning of October, but we had a large number of wounded men that were thrown out of action, about 420 soldiers who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned individuals in the joint command and the units, we can say, in fact, that they were Muslim/Croat units and a Muslim/Croat command; is that true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was a command in Zavidovici and in Maglaj and in Usora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the Jajce front for a moment because in October, Jajce was to fall. When you said that you organised the 80 kilometres in sectors, for example, at every 8 kilometres there would be one commander in charge of one sector, were these sectors left to the defence of the local people in the villages or were you able to coordinate with the municipalities in Central Bosnia and have them take part in the defence of Jajce? What was that like?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not possible to ensure that the entire front line at that town was organised and defended with their own forces alone because it is an enormous territory. We succeeded in having from the other municipalities, we engaged per week between 50 and 100 recruits from the other municipalities, and we formed and equipped a unit, a Croat/Muslim unit, which was called the Kotor Varos Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Croatian/Muslim unit, under which composition was that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was under the composition of the HVO, came under the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the beginning of the end of Jajce; that is to say, the beginning of the fall of Jajce, when did that occur, and what, in your opinion, was one of the reasons that Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The beginning of the downfall of Jajce came with the intensification of the conflict in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That was on the 19th, that is to say, the night between the 18th and 19th of October, 1992. The conflict broke out between the Territorial Defence and the Croatian Defence Council in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The reason for that conflict was, once again, the petrol pump, the gas station, and efforts made to take control of the building of the old hotel, the old hotel building and other facilities in town by the TO; they wanted to take control. We were not able, from that day onwards, to send a convoy with ammunition and materiel to Jajce because the convoy was stopped in Opara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which municipality is Opara in?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Opara is in the Novi Travnik municipality under the control of the Territorial Defence of Novi Travnik (indicating). That was a convoy that I went to Mostar to ensure on the 19th of October, 1992. In addition to the impossibility of sending a convoy to the area, the shifts that were to have been sent out from Kakanj and Vares to the Jajce area did not manage to pass through from the 20th of October because this was not permitted by the Territorial Defence from Kakanj, and they set up checkpoints, roadblocks, to stop them passing on the main road. The shifts from Kiseljak and Kresevo, to assist the defenders as backup for the defenders of Jajce, which had managed to pass in the afternoon hours of the 20th of October, were stopped in Karaula, and the shifts that were already in Jajce remained in Jajce, but I think that this merely speeded up the fall of Jajce because it upset morale amongst the soldiers and it upset a situation of cooperation which had existed between the Territorial Defence and HOS in Jajce and the HVO. Jajce was in a complete semi-encirclement by the Serbian army, and it was very difficult to defend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 26th of October, 1992; that is considered to be the beginning of the fall of Jajce. Could you give us, in chronological terms, an overview of the more important events from the 26th onwards so that we can see what the fall of Jajce was like and what the results of that were on the overall situation in Central Bosnia and particularly in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of October, we were subjected to heavy shelling, and one of our positions fell. It is called the Gola Planina, as well as another position called Vrbica, and that signalled the fall of the entire area of Jajce. As early as the 27th of October, the Serbs drove out about 4.000 civilians who had been displaced persons from Kotor Varos, and they sent them towards Travnik. This caused further complications for us because now we needed to care for four (sic) more displaced persons who, in the course of this day, all arrived in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four thousand.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Four thousand refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we place on the ELMO Exhibit D260 (sic), this has to do with Jajce, so we can see where Jajce was and what the front looked like just before the fall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These 4.000 refugees, what was their nationality? General Blaskic, what was the nationality of the 4.000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: There were both Croats and Muslims, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. The correct Exhibit number is D160.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Show Jajce and Zenica just so we can get oriented. All of these areas were under the control of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The light areas were under the control of the Bosnian army, and the darker ones were under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Here's Jajce, Zenica -- I'm showing Zenica now for orientation -- and we received the refugees, the displaced persons who had been displaced from Kotor Varos (indicating), who arrived via Skender Vakuf and Vlasic and finally reached Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pass, was it a corridor, and how big was this corridor through which you can enter and exit Jajce immediately before the fall?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The corridor was narrowed to the point where one could shoot through the corridor, one could fire from one end to the other with a simple rifle. It was 200 metres. At this one point, which is called Vocnjak, you could only pass through at night. You would have to prepare vehicles with -- you couldn't use the lights, and you still ran the risk of having some of the vehicles shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? When did the next group of civilians move towards the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 28th, the entire population was mobilised, everybody who lived in the Jajce municipality. This comprised at least 25.000 people, including civilians and soldiers, and they all started moving towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these civilians and soldiers in terms of their ethnic origins?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were Croats and Bosniak Muslims, and there were about equal numbers of each of these two groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you engaged in after the 28th and how did the situation develop?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We tried to use this corridor and provide as much assistance as we could. This was up until the 28th. We had some casualties alongside this corridor, so for a while this road was completely blocked because the Serbs had hit two vehicles on the road, on the section of the road between Travnik and Karaula, and there we had casualties. On the 28th, I personally attempted, along with General Prkacin and about 300 volunteers which he had brought along, this was a battalion which was called Zmajod Bosne, which is called "Bosnian Dragon," and we tried to break through towards Jajce. We had started but the road was completely jammed with refugees who were streaming from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here that Jajce was almost completely surrounded. Did the population panic, and did the panic cause the entire population to start moving?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that panic was one of the causes, perhaps a certain lack of mutual confidence, and it contributed to the early fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You addressed the population at Jajce. What was the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Travnik, but let me just clarify that at that time the situation in Travnik was becoming desperate for us because a further attack from the Serbian army was a risk, which would have been a continuation of this major success of theirs. So three days passed between the 28th and the 31st, and the refugees were still in the streets of Travnik, in Vitez, and in Novi Travnik. I was asked by their representatives to hear them out, and on the 31st of October, in front of the -- it was either the elementary or the high school, I addressed these refugees who were complaining about not having received any bread for three days and other food stocks, clothes, and that they were left without any care. A similar thing also happened in Vitez, the problems were similar, but the demands by these masses of refugees were different. One group demanded passage to third countries, and the other group demanded to be temporarily accommodated in this area of Central Bosnia. Also, law and order all but broke down because, due to the fact that the civilian authorities and police were not functioning and unable to meet the needs of such a large number of refugees, the refugees were selling -- bartering their weapons and military equipment in order to get means for their survival. In Karaula (indicating) and along -- via Turbe and to Travnik, they organised checkpoints, these were barricades, and at these checkpoints, all the military recruits who were armed were being disarmed. So the situation was very chaotic in the area. There were even conflicts between the expelled Croats from Jajce and the Croats in Novi Travnik, armed conflicts, that is, and a number of incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The checkpoint of the Territorial Defence at Karaula, was that point one of the points where these weapons were being taken away and collected?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: According to the report which I received, at this checkpoint about 2.386 rifles were taken away from members of the Jajce HVO as well as ten truckloads, mostly -- ten trucks. These were not military trucks, these were civilian trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These were the members of the TO in Karaula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the fall of Jajce, a new front line was established at Travnik. Could you explain what your involvement was with this new front line?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Starting on the 28th of October, I spent most of my time in Travnik because now a new front had been created, and our assessment was that the Serbian army was going to continue to exploit their success in Jajce and try to conquer more territory in the Travnik municipality. I tried to organise a defence of the Travnik municipality in the areas which we considered would be targeted for the first combat operations. I also established a command post there, and on one of the positions, I also had my own command post. The situation was fairly complex, and refugees from Jajce made the whole situation even worse because they were projecting this feeling that the Serbian advances could not be stopped. For me, at that time, survival was of paramount importance because if we lost Travnik, we would have nothing left to defend in the Lasva Valley. I held a number of meetings with Dzemo Merdan who, at that time, was the commander of the regional staff in Zenica, and we tried to reach an agreement on the organisation of the defence of the town of Travnik. At first, we did this again by sectors, and later we managed, through the joint command, to establish joint defence teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what happened to these civilians or ex-soldiers and their families who had come from Jajce, I mean both Croats and Muslims? Did some of them stay? Did some of them move on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The majority of Croats who were expelled left the area of Central Bosnia while the majority of Muslims, of Muslim refugees, remained, and at first they were accommodated in the Travnik barracks, and later on, in other municipalities in Central Bosnia, that is Vitez, Zenica, and other municipalities. Also, at first we managed to keep a certain number of soldiers of the Kotor Varos Battalion, but even this unit split up so that the Bosniak Muslims joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the HVO, with their families, left together with the other refugees from Jajce, they left Central Bosnia. A few of them stayed behind, maybe ten to twenty soldiers, and before this Kotor Varos Battalion was dissolved, it numbered 500 to 600 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a Croatian/Muslim unit within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you worked with Merdan on the organisation of defence of Travnik. I'm not going to take you to all the details about the military organisation, but I would like the usher to put Exhibit number D347 on the ELMO. I would like you to tell us about this document, the circumstances under which this order of yours was issued.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This order was issued following a meeting on the 4th of November, 1992, which I had with Dzemo Merdan, and General Merdan asked of me in this meeting to issue an order literally for the reasons which are set out in item number 1 of this order, that is, to prevent setting fire to houses of eminent citizens of Muslim nationalities in Travnik. After the end of the conflict in Travnik, we had established a joint commission which worked until the 4th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, this order here refers to Novi Travnik because in the transcript it says "Travnik"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is Novi Travnik. The commission was established to investigate the causes and ascertain the consequences of this conflict, and it completed its work on the 4th of November. Despite the fact that it ceased work because of the one-sided refusal by the TO to continue the work, Dzemo and I still tried to stabilise this situation through documents like this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the incident about? How did this setting afire take place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Houses were being set on fire, this usually happened at night, and the structures that were targeted were mostly those belonging to the prominent citizens of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you issued another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I please have Exhibit D400 placed an the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall this document and the circumstances under which it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This also followed the meeting on the 4th of November with Dzemo Merdan, but it refers to different problems in the territory of the Vitez municipality, and what I wanted with this document was to improve the cooperation and eliminate all misunderstandings in relation to the members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, the Travnik municipality defence had stabilised. The Serbs were stopped; the advances of the Serbs were stopped for the first time. Were you able to secure assistance of all municipal staffs at that time? Could you just briefly explain?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This was the only way for us to stabilise the front in Travnik; in other words, we tasked the municipal staffs in Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, Vares, and Kakanj, Zenica, Busovaca, and Vitez with this front; in other words, each municipal staff was tasked with defending one segment of the front. This was the only way for us to stop further advances of the Serbian army and protect the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, on 14 December, you helped the 2nd army corps in Tuzla with ammunition and weapons. Can you describe what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Simultaneously with this, there were intense combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd corps of the BH army, and a request reached us from their headquarters asking for assistance. We did so on a regular basis, and we did so this time too. This wasn't the only time when we sent a significant amount of ammunition, which they were in need of in order to defend themselves. The assistance was sent to the BH army, to the 2nd corps, that is, to the regional staff in Tuzla. This is how it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us leave aside the front lines because the Travnik front line was stabilised, and the Serbs couldn't break through. Let me take you to another area. Your other major responsibility, earlier today, you said that your main responsibilities were the front and the other one was the organisation of the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber, when you took over this duty, how was the HVO, or what was called the HVO, organised, and how did you proceed about organising an army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: By taking over my duties, I, in fact, found an armed people and armed villagers in the different municipalities, and it was the municipal staff that functioned. It would, of course, have been more usual and normal had I had an organised army with which I would be able to engage in combat operations at the front; however, my priority task was to organise defence, and in addition to that task, I had to organise the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, according to your overall military knowledge, professional knowledge, is this the usual kind of situation, that is to say, that the operative commander has to create, to organise an army? Is that something that is standard practice in warfare?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is not, and it is, first and foremost, the task of the state institutions, the Ministry of Defence and so on and the other kindred institutions, it is their task to organise and form armies. A commander is there to see to the deployment and use of that army, at least in wartime. I had municipal commands which were organised in completely different ways and which, unfortunately, did not have any basis for an existing organisation, so that I had to spend a great deal of time and effort to elaborate drafts for organisation, organisational drafts, and other supplementary documents which we could use as the groundwork, as the basis, for setting up, forming, organising military formations, and we spent all our energy in trying to create military formations, smaller ones and then bigger ones, but in addition to our efforts and the many documents that we had, this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A meeting, at which you discussed the organisation of the army on the 16th of October, 1992, was attended by the Prime Minister of Herceg-Bosna, Jadranko Prlic. What happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was a meeting that I was invited to attend as well, and the conclusion was that the HVO was not organised militarily, that they were non-mobile village units, that the municipalities, with their municipal army, were prevalent, and he also said that, as far as the military police was concerned and the security service was concerned, those two services were solely responsible to their own commands. He concluded, in particular, that the HVO had no operative units, nor did it have an elaborated system of organisation by which to create those units and form those units, and at that meeting, he emphasised that power and authority, and he had in mind civilian power and authority, must be shared with the Bosniak Muslims in relation to the electoral results and the proportions of the population, which the results were already known. He also stressed, with respect to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that it was only a provisional solution, a temporary one, and that it was not its goal to overthrow the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that its duty was to defend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these attempts to create an army, there was a vital reorganisation that took place, that is to say, you were under the joint command of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you explain how this occurred? Where were you informed that you were no longer the actual commander, and what happened generally?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of November, while I was still in Travnik, I was informed by my assistant that, in Busovaca, a press conference had been held by the defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Bozo Rajic. At that press conference, he stressed that a joint command had been set up for the 3rd corps and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and that the commanders, who had been appointed to head the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were Mr. Arif Pasalic and, to represent the HVO, General Ante Prkacin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Arif Pasalic was a Muslim, was he not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ante Prkacin, what ethnicity was he? Can you tell us a few words about him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was a HOS general and an army general of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that he was a Croat by way of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of November, 1992, I attended a reception at Mr. Bruno Stojic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function did he hold?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: He was the representative of the defence department of Herceg-Bosna, and he confirmed that Commanders Arif Pasalic and Mr. Prkacin were responsible for the 3rd corps and the Operative Zone and that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. The Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: And also that a number of officers had been designated in the joint command engaged in the security service and the information service and information activities and the military intelligence service. This information and the presentation by Bruno Stojic, I understood as my replacement, that I had been replaced, and I agreed to that. I confirmed that, with that decision, I no longer had the function of the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Bruno Stojic told me that he did not want to accept a solution and proposal of this kind, and he asked me to place myself at the disposal of the joint command and to offer my assistance and services and work according to the tasks and assignments of General Prkacin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps we can take a break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We may resume the hearing. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we stopped where Bruno Stojic had informed you of the existence of a joint command and that you offered your resignation which he did not accept. What did he tell you your duties would be in future?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Bruno Stojic told me that I should report to General Prkacin in Travnik and place myself at the disposal of General Prkacin and work according to his assignments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned and, of course, contacted General Prkacin. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: General Prkacin told me that he had convened a meeting for the 8th of November, 1992 in Travnik, at which he wanted to become acquainted with the situation, and he wanted the commanders of the municipal staff to report to him on the situation; however, the commanders at that meeting refused to report on the situation and refused to obey him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next with regard to the organisation of the army? You still had the municipal staff. When did you form the units, the brigades? When did you equip your staff, and when did you take up residence in the Hotel Vitez? When did you set up headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Once we were given this joint command, I first sent officers, at the request of General Prkacin, to the joint command so as to set up teams, and after that, I was engaged in filling the command for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone with manpower. From the 25th of November onwards, we endeavoured to set up the brigades, but this was a reappointment of the former municipal commands, that is to say, they became the brigades and an attempt to improve, in that way, the effectiveness of our defence and to mitigate the municipal approach, that is to say, each municipality was isolated and considered that it was sufficient on its own, so we tried to militarise this overall composition of our recruits. Of course, the very fact that some brigades were formed in the space of only four days speaks for itself and shows that it was a renaming, in fact, of the municipal staff which then became the HVO brigades. At the end of November, I received approval and permission from the head of the main staff, two of the staff, to have the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone set up a headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, and we took up residence in two premises in the Hotel Vitez. Our offices were denoted as offices A-1 and A-2 in the hotel, and there was a little small bar in the hotel which we took over, whereas the whole of the rest of the hotel was used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't follow this. Were you confirmed as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone? Excuse me. I didn't really understand. You said that you wanted to resign, General Prkacin said that you could not, and then the interpreter said that the municipal commanders didn't obey that, and then suddenly you talked about municipalities and brigades. Were you confirmed in your assignment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you explain that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: From the 8th of November onwards, I was responsible to Mr. Prkacin, and Prkacin, at that particular time, was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. But that was on the 8th of November; you were confirmed then, is that -- he gave you the Operative Zone to be under your responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In November, Prkacin commanded the entire area of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and at that first meeting held on the 8th of November, the commanders of the municipal staff refused to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I understood that from the transcript. But then afterwards, exactly what is the very specific way that you became -- you assumed the official position of the municipal brigade which had been turned into a brigade? They didn't obey, and then what happened officially when there was no obedience?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They refused to obey for that particular day, that is to say, they did not report to him, but they continued to cooperate with Commander Prkacin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I really don't understand. I ask you the question -- General Prkacin was not obeyed. They refused to obey him. I do understand that. They refused to give the information to obey. But you, what officially did you become?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The second man in the command of the Operative Zone, so either Prkacin's deputy or chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's what I didn't understand. That was the piece that was missing. That had not been made clear. You were confirmed as No. 2 for Prkacin who was the chief of staff in Central Bosnia. Is that right, Mr. Nobilo? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but no orders were issued in that respect. The Minister of Defence had just said, "Place yourself under Prkacin."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To make a situation that was not entirely clear, to make it entirely clear, because it is our position the situation was not entirely clear at the time. You had new players being stuck in with no clear guidance being given to the accused as to what his job was, what his function was, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. I was looking for a clarification and I needed it because I did not really see the connection between the accused, who says that "I'm going to resign," and then for Prkacin, he says he's resigning, the other person says, "No, stay," and then the municipal headquarters don't obey, and then suddenly the accused is organising the headquarters in Vitez and he would remain the commander of the Operative Zone. I was missing a link there. I don't like to interrupt, but when I do, I'm looking for clarifications. Otherwise, we are not going to have to ask the question two or three weeks from now. I apologise for interrupting. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, the situation was indeed a confusing one, but it was what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, regardless of Prkacin, who, in the joint command was your superior, and Pascalic was also your superior, they were commanders of an equal standing, you, at the level of the Operative Zone, continued to work with the formation and organisation. Did you do anything with the organisation of the headquarters, new rules, equipment, and so on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In addition to this order, I compiled the first draft of the rules for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone where I defined the structure of command and the competencies and authority of the individual sections of the command, that is to say, a description of the jobs, so to speak, within the command itself. Sometime at the beginning of December, within the composition of the Operative Zone, Mr. Franjo Nakic joined us, and he took over duties of the chief of staff of the Operative Zone. I also organised a seminar with members of the Operative Zone staff. It was a lecture through which I wanted to inform them of what was expected of them, what their duties were, what their competencies were, and what methods the command would use in its daily functioning and functioning on a month-by-month basis, because most of the members of the command of the Operative Zone were, for the most part, of other professions. They were not active military men, most of them. I also went round the municipal headquarters, I toured them and held lectures as to organisational matters and method of functioning of the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the organisation and functioning, something important happened on the 13th of December, 1992, and what happened would have a direct effect on the events incorporated in the indictment. It refers to the reorganisation of the military police. Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what this meeting was on the 13th of December, 1992, and could we have a chart of the organisation of the Herceg-Bosna Community and place it on the ELMO, please, with the help of the usher? The document is D167A. Before we go on to look at the chart, would you describe the meeting of the 13th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I had a meeting with the head of the main staff in the Vitez office, and I was visited there by the representatives of the military police administration from Mostar. Mr. Lovric came, the deputy head of the military police department, Mr. Barbaric, came, the assistant head of the military police administration, and Mr. Mustapic, the commander of the 1st Battalion, active battalion, of the regional military police from Mostar. With them came the commander of the regional company of the military police from Vitez, Mr. Pasko Ljubicic. The topic of that meeting was the reorganisation of the military police, and the main question, the main issue that we discussed, was the question of command over the military police. The gentlemen from the military police administration in Mostar, to me and General Petkovic, presented their views, that according to the new set-up, the new organisation, the military police in Vitez would be commanded solely by the military police administration, and the first regional company of the military police which was deployed in Vitez by formation and structure was the 1st active battalion of the regional military police from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, shall we translate this into layman's language and try to explain it better? Did I understand you correctly? The 1st company of the military police in Vitez was part of the 1st Battalion of the military police of Mostar; is that correct? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 1st company of the military police in Vitez at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, the commander of the 1st company of the military police was Mr. Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along with this 1st active company of the military police commanded by Pasko Ljubicic and which was part of the battalion in Mostar, was there a regional military police in Central Bosnia, and if so, how was that organised?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th Battalion existed of the regional military police in Central Bosnia which was organised into companies which themselves were deployed in the different municipalities of Central Bosnia, and its commander was Zvonko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these two kinds of military police, was there a third military police which existed there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were municipal military police forces, but they were much smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, what did the representatives of the military police administration tell you and Mr. Pasko how were you going to be able to use these forces? In other words, who was going to be the commander of the military police and to whom were the police units answerable?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The military police was subordinated to the chief of the military police administration, and the commander of the regional military police company was Pasko Ljubicic. The commander of the 4th Battalion was Zvonko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, how could you use the military police? What were you told? What was the organisation within this overall structure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was told that I could in no way issue orders and command the military police. I could only send a request through the main staff to the military police administration, and the military police administration would consider this request and would issue orders to the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position, that is, General Petkovic's and your own position with respect to what you were told in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We both said -- first I said so, that this was an unnatural type of operation and that because -- primarily because of the lack of communication lines, this police force was not going to be efficient in the area of Central Bosnia, and General Petkovic also said that this would be an introduction of parallel commands or dual commands and that this could in no way function in the area of Central Bosnia because very frequently there are no communications so that I could send requests for any type of involvement of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the representatives of the military police administration accept this objection that you and General Petkovic made or did they abide by their position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They did not accept our arguments, and they said that it was going to be the way they decided, in other words, what they said was going to be the rule regardless of our objections because they had written documents on rules which they received from the defence department. There was a book regulating the command structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your understanding that this document gave them this authority of command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding, that this document permitted them to maintain this type of functioning of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience and your knowledge from the JNA, were these things functioning in a similar way in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No. In the JNA, you had unity of command and unity of responsibility, which meant that in a single area there is a single commander and that he commands all forces. For instance, a commander of a brigade in the JNA had direct command over the military police company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did they have the HVO model or the JNA model?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course I know what they had because I had a number of meetings with the commander of the 3rd corps and his deputy. The commander of the 3rd corps had direct command of a battalion of the military police, it was called a corps military police battalion, and he also had direct command over a military police company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This may be a good moment to explain to the Trial Chamber in, let's say, a normal, regular army, what does it mean for a commander to have the use of military police for his functioning as a commander? In other words, what is the importance, what is the significance of being able to use military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This would be an instrument to implement certain orders and it would be a force which provides the power to a commander or an ability to sanction insubordination, failure to follow certain orders or certain rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you take away this power from a commander, that is, to use military police, what is his command reduced to in case of soldiers who do not carry out orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: There are two consequences. First, people may not know, but they will soon find out that he doesn't have that power; and secondly, then everything is reduced to convincing or repeating the same order, and you are reduced to using general authority which any single individual may have in relation to his associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To sum up, without the use of military police, can a commander essentially perform his commanding duties, militarily speaking? Can he successfully command without the use of military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Command and control is not efficient if a commander is not given the use of military force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let me interrupt for a moment, please, Mr. Nobilo. General Blaskic, as regards this change, in your opinion, is it really a change of command, of parallel command, or a radical change? There could be many explanations for that. At least those people who were responsible did not see that they were taking command power away, or was it that they had any other type of objective? In your opinion, what did this mean, this new change of parallel command? What was the purpose of it for those people who came to that decision? What is your opinion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know what the purpose was, what the motives were of the people who took away this power, but I know what the consequences were for any commander who faced this radical change. The command power was significantly reduced, and worst of all, a parallel command was introduced so that now, in a single area, we had a person who is responsible for consequences for behaviour, for mistakes, if you will, because the police can make mistakes, and two or more persons who have the right to command and also have sort of an overall responsibility for what is going on in the area. I wrote about this and I talked with the UN representatives who were there, with the former European Monitors, in an attempt to learn whether there were any other examples elsewhere, and they themselves were surprised that this type of system of functioning was in place. It looked unnatural to everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's identify the person who formally was responsible for what happened in Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else had independent command in the area of Central Bosnia apart from you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I don't know which unit you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police was the commander of the 4th Battalion, Zvonko Vukovic, and also the commander of the regional military police, Mr. Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on -- we will touch on the issue whether, apart from the military police and the HVO brigades, there were other chains of command, apart from you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an additional chain of command which was independent of me. These were the special purpose units which were used even on the front lines, battlefronts, and without my being informed of that. For instance, at the time of the fall of Jajce and when I was there with all the manpower I had available, one of these units was deployed in southern Herzegovina at the Stolac front, and I wasn't even informed that they would go, that they went, or that they came back when they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps, just for the record, two documents, 517 and 518 which are under seal, D517 and D518.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the level of the Operative Zone and the military police top, was the same situation reflected in lower levels? You had a meeting on that regard in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a problem in Kiseljak, there was a problem in Zepce between the commanders of the newly-formed brigades and commanders of the military police, and this was a conflict over the competence in Kiseljak. The only thing I could do to reconcile the positions of two commanders, on the one hand the brigade commander in Kiseljak and the commander of the military police on the other hand, was that on 16th of December, I organised a meeting, together with Mr. Pasko Ljubicic, commander of the military police, and we reached a compromise consisting of the fact that the commander of the brigade did not have the right to control the military police in the carrying out of its daily duties or have command over it in Kiseljak, they could only review the premises which they occupied, and the commander of the military police company in Kiseljak could use the Kiseljak barracks where the main command -- the chief commander was commander of the brigade, or the case in Zepce was, and this was repeated, the commander of the military police would be in charge of the entire command staff, including Ivo Lozancic, the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is all for the organisation and structure today. These were your two key tasks in 1992. I want to move into another area which is your assessment of the relations between Muslims and Croats, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the HVO. Can you first tell me, in general terms, yesterday we saw that there were a number of incidents, you referred to a number of them, and today we will just refer to a few of them, in your opinion, what was the cause of this growing friction between Muslims and Croats in 1992, that is? We're only talking about 1992 now. If you can, in general terms, tell us, what were the sources of conflicts between these two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course, there were a number of causes, but one of them was a huge influx of refugees. These were desperate people. Unfortunately, many of them were armed, and because of the inability of the civilian authorities to care for them, they had to fend for themselves as victims of aggression, sometimes even using the methods used on them when they were expelled from their homes. So they sometimes engaged in robberies, they harassed the local population in the areas where they settled, and engaged in different kinds of criminal activities to secure their survival. Of course, such incidents caused mistrust, fear, but as the situation on the front was becoming more complex, it became easier for us to reach agreements and to overcome this mistrust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I mean the HVO, that is, the Operative Zone, and the 3rd corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in your view, the misunderstandings and conflicts within the Muslim and Croat civilian authorities also had some effect on the general split between the Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was another cause because the civilian authorities, in my view, operated in terms of personalities. That means that in all municipalities, in Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, and I'm not going to go on, the civilian authorities were minding their own group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the Croatian authorities took care of and felt responsible for their own people. That had to do with collecting taxes, use of the civilian police. I remember well certain meetings which I had with the commander of the 3rd corps when he repeated to me, he repeatedly said, and I quote him, "The problem here is not the army," meaning the Operative Zone and the 3rd corps. "The problem here is the dual government which is functioning," and I think that the Washington Agreement also testifies to that. The relations between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Central Bosnia and the HVO, in military terms, this agreement between the two sides was reached very easily following the Washington Accords. Military recruits, which made up the 3rd corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, were all living in the areas of these municipalities with this dual government function. So let me put it simply: Within a week, each civilian would be a soldier for one day and a civilian for six days, and the functioning of the civilian authorities definitely had an effect on him in such living conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that there were two governments, a Muslim and a Croatian, and they were all looking after their own people, are you saying that, in 1992, there was -- in territorial terms, did this division reflect the state of affairs? In other words, were they overlapping on the same territory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean in practical terms? Let's say as regards taxes, for instance, collecting taxes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, taxes were collected by the HVO government in Vitez from Croatian citizens who lived in the territory of the Vitez municipality, and the government or, as it was called, the War Presidency of this same municipality, that is, the Vitez municipality, but in another area of the municipality, that is, in old Vitez, they collected it from the Muslim citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "old Vitez," this is where their headquarters was, but from which area did they collect taxes from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: From the entire territory of the Vitez municipality in places where Muslims lived, that is, the citizens who were Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this mean, having two governments in the same territory in terms of police? Who was in charge of the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you've tried, but it isn't too clear to me. I wonder if you'd ask the witness to clarify your line of questioning a little more on the previous phase. You have a geographical unit, say, Stari Vitez, old Vitez. Now, would the HVO in Vitez collect taxes from everybody in Vitez, whether Muslims or Croats; likewise, would the BiH collect taxes from everybody in Stari Vitez, whether Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What you just asked is a key question, but I'd like to avoid confusion. Old Vitez is not crucial. This is where the Muslim War Presidency headquarters was, but we have the Vitez municipality in its territory, and now I'll let the witness say this:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the HVO government collect the taxes from, it being part of the HVO government, and from whom did the War Presidency collect taxes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The Vitez municipality HVO government collected taxes from all citizens in the territory of the Vitez municipality, and the War Presidency of the Bosniak Muslims collected taxes from Bosniak Muslims, of all citizens who were Bosniak Muslims in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One key point is missing. The HVO government in Vitez is collecting taxes from all Croatian citizens in the territory of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it is missing from the record. The Muslim War Presidency, that is, the wartime government --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, is collecting taxes from all Bosniak Muslims in the territory of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This principle of dual government relating to the citizens of one or the other nationality or ethnicity, was it present and evident in other activities as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It existed in other realms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the police? We have one or two police forces at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We had a police force which was commanded by the government of the HVO Vitez in the area of the Vitez municipality, and we also had a police force commanded by the wartime presidency of the municipality of Vitez composed of Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these two civilian authorities, even if they were autonomous, did they recognise different central authorities, central governments, or different higher authorities than the municipality authorities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, they recognised two different central powers, different from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did they recognise? The Muslim wartime presidency of Vitez, who did it recognise?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It recognised exclusively the wartime presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the municipal government of Vitez? Who was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The municipal government of Vitez was subordinated to the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this division in civilian authority and the division of political ideas generate conflicts between nations, ethnic groups, in the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course it generated this because I already said that most of the time military recruits spent at home living in the territory of this type of municipality having that dual authority and dual government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your competencies, whether factual or legal, according to the laws of Herceg-Bosna, as a commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, your competencies and authorisations, did they incorporate any part of civilian life, that is to say, did you have any influence on the civilian organs of power and authority and the political decisions that were made?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony, I said that I was not known in my own municipality, I was a stranger to those parts, so I did not have any political ambitions, nor was I specially interested in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wield any influence on the decisions made by the civilian organs, whether Muslim or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any competency over civilian life, official competency?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1992, I spent the whole of 1992, in fact, trying to realise the competencies and authority invested in me by the rules of Herceg-Bosna as the operative commander of Central Bosnia, those I was entitled to. I tried to take them over from the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you have another question about this particular aspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps just one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What functions did you endeavour to take away from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Only military functions, exclusively military functions that the municipality had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of the law or in actual fact, at any point in time covered by the indictment, were you the military commander or governor, so to speak, of civilian Bosnia, that is to say, the key figure of overall life in the region, civilian and military?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, never. I never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If you would like a break now, this is perhaps a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Mr. Nobilo, please continue with your questions, the questions you want to ask the witness, and continue until 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more sentence on the matter we were discussing before the break. You already mentioned something, quoting Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd corps, how do you assess the relationship between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, the 3rd corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We had already established a joint command from the 3rd -- that is to say, the 4th of November, 1992 and especially on the fronts that I enumerated for November and December. We had command teams, joint command teams, linked up, and I consider that the relationships were fairly good and that cooperation in 1992 was fairly good. With the commander of the 3rd corps, for example, I would tour some of the military factories so as to set the example. The two of us setting the example would show the workers in the factory that this kind of cooperation was both necessary and possible, feasible. I attended meetings at the command headquarters of the 3rd corps, and also the command came to us for Christmas in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to 1993, for purposes of illustration and the record, could you perhaps mention some incidents which would throw more light on the situation as it existed in the area?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: There were quite a number of incidents, and they occurred both in November and in December, and I'm going to enumerate just a few of those incidents. On the 10th of November in Zepce, during the meeting of the civilian authorities of Zepce, the HVO, one of the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina threw a hand grenade at the building where the meeting was being convened. Then there was another serious incident on the 15th of November, 1992 when Mr. Dzemo Merdan was arrested, taken into custody, and taken to my office in the Hotel Vitez where General Prkacin was there, together with me. Mr. Dzemo Merdan was taken prisoner by the commander of the Vitezovi, and we succeeded, after a lot of convincing, to have him freed, and he was given back his equipment. Then in Kakanj in mid November, there was another incident where the members of the Territorial Defence and members of the Croatian Defence Council from Kakanj itself directed their weapons and took up combat deployment facing each other, opposite each other. Also in mid November in Novi Travnik, fortifications were built by the Territorial Defence, and they were facing Croatian villages. I reacted on that occasion as well and asked the command in Novi Travnik not to interfere with the digging of trenches. I did not wish to create problems in regard to these activities. On the 18th of November in Travnik, the deputy commander of the Travnik HVO was killed. His name was Mr. Nikola Grbesa. In the night between the 18th and 19th of November in Vitez, a soldier belonging to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was killed, and as a reaction to this, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Vitez took prisoner nine regional military policemen in retaliation and subjected them to a certain amount of torture and maltreatment. On the 21st of November in Travnik, an officer of the main staff was killed, main staff of the HVO, for links and communication with UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was the liaison officer, and he was killed. There were other individual killings as well, such as a case that occurred in Novi Travnik where the killers -- the perpetrators went into territory under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They went to Gornji Vakuf. There were also other individual cases, vice versa, that is to say, if the killer was a man from Gornji Vakuf, then he would flee to a territory under the control of the HVO and so avoid any action taken against him. At the beginning of December, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Novi Travnik took control of a primary school in the village of Vodavod and stopped our shifts going to the front to face the army of the Republika Srpska. A similar problem was mentioned yesterday in Kiseljak when we talked about the village of Duhri. In mid December, at the Pasinac feature about Zenica, trenches were dug facing the Croatian villages and Croatian houses. Then, after that, on the 28th of December, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Travnik sent a combat unit to take possession of the hospital there and took over a ward, a wing of the hospital, in Travnik. By taking up these positions on the premises of the hospital, Travnik was placed under military supervision of that particular unit of the BH army. At the end of December, we had difficulties because, despite our efforts to -- that is, despite the efforts of the BH army to take over control of part of the front facing the army of the Republika Srpska in Novi Travnik, we did not succeed in this; that is to say, the complete front line in Novi Travnik was still under the control of the HVO. An incident that lasted a little longer and which was worrying us, gave rise to anxiety in the Croatian Defence Council and the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia, had become evident, that is to say, the operative development of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the 3rd corps, went in-depth within the territory or behind the front lines. There was a grouping of brigades, such as the 306th Brigade in Han Bila and the Travnik municipality, the 308th Brigade in Novi Travnik, and the other units in the Lasva Valley which were not engaged at the front line facing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the formation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army was formed in-depth of the territory, what do you mean by the depth of the territory compared to the front? What is the "in-depth" term that you use?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Everything that goes from the shelter of the soldiers up at the front line, everything else is the rear, everything behind the soldier's back is the rear and the depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, on Mount Vlasic, we have those two flags. Give us an example. What, compared to the front line of Vlasic, is the rear, the depth of the territory which is where the BH army was grouped?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On Vlasic, we had forces, army forces and HVO forces in Travnik as well, from this line, front line here, towards Vitez, Zenica, and Busovaca (indicating), and all that was the rear, the depth of the territory. Let me explain this in a different way. That is the front line (indicating), so everything behind it or west of that pointer is the depth of the territory. It was cause for anxiety, and we wondered why forces were being accumulated in Novi Travnik, why there was a grouping of forces in Novi Travnik. There were about two and a half thousand soldiers being grouped there if they were not engaged on a single metre of the Novi Travnik front facing the Republika Srpska army. Also, similarly, why was the 306th Brigade in Han Bila if there were no positions for the defence of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this worried you. Now, after a period of time had passed, what did you conclude? What was the operative function and goal of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, I discussed this matter first with General Merdan, the deputy commander of the 3rd corps, when, at one of the meetings held in November, he asked me for my assistance and to help him put up 6.000 to 7.000 soldiers in Travnik, about 2.500 soldiers in Novi Travnik, and about 2.300 soldiers in Vitez belonging to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I asked him why, what this army was to be used for if it was not to be engaged at the front, and he said that he was working on organisational matters, to organise the operative forces of the 3rd Corps. I had the same type of meeting on the 21st of December in Zenica in the headquarters of the 3rd corps when the commander of the 3rd corps himself, Enver Hadzihasanovic, asked me to mediate, together with him, with the civilian authorities to mobilise the buildings for our purposes in which we could put up soldiers. I was to mediate with the representatives of the civilian authorities, the Croat civilian authorities, and the soldiers belonged to the BH army.
