I told Enver on the occasion, Enver who was the commander of the 3rd corps, I told him that there was enough space at Mount Vlasic and at the front lines for us to engage such a large number of soldiers, and he repeated the answer that I was given by Dzemo as well, that is, he said that he was setting up a corps and an operative brigade. Later on, I came to realise that this operative development enabled very effective use and engagement of forces of the BH army against the HVO in the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For the moment, in this stage of the testimony, we would conclude with the 1992 events and move on to 1993. Mr. President, as most of the indictment, the time span of the indictment, is concentrated in the first four or five months of 1993, we shall be moving along in chronological order, taking it day by day and reconstructing those months. It is the view of Defence counsel that the indictment is not precise enough, and in a situation of that kind, we have been forced to reconstruct the events in chronological order so as to provide the Trial Chamber with sufficient facts upon which to draw its conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's move on to 1993, and let's try to make a chronological reconstruction of what took place that year. So go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1993, I started from Kiseljak to Vitez to go to the Hotel Vitez, to the command post of the Operative Zone. In the Brestovsko local commune (indicating) -- so in the Brestovsko local commune, I was stopped by -- I was stopped by the assistant for security, Mr. Anto Sliskovic, who arrived from Vitez via Busovaca, and he arrived in Brestovsko, and I had started from my birthplace -- I mean from my home in Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information did he have with him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: He told me that it wouldn't be good for me to continue with this trip to Hotel Vitez because an incident had taken place, and what happened was that a military policeman named Mato Jakovljevic attempted to execute me and Commander Pasko. After this military policeman opened fire in the hallways of the Hotel Vitez and forcibly opened the door to my office, he threw in a hand grenade in the hallway in front of the office, probably assuming that I was in the office. After this, this policeman, Jakovljevic, left the hotel, came back, and then the hotel security shot and killed him, and Sliskovic also informed me that the tensions rose in Vitez as a consequence of this event because the policemen among themselves started arguing whether Jakovljevic was or was not to be killed. In any event, I went back that day, and again in the afternoon Sliskovic told me not to come to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Move on to -- what else in January in 1993 happened that was of particular significance?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, logistics was a major problem, as it was throughout December, and I ordered Ivica Cobanac, who was at Sebesic, to return all the equipment to the 110th Usora Brigade. This equipment had been taken away illegally from the convoy, and in the morning briefing, I asked the regional military police to review the security of the hotel and to make necessary replacements of personnel, and I also ordered a complete investigation of the event of the 1st of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we are at this, this may be good to point out, that after you and Petkovic met with the military police authorities and you disagreed with the procedures which were forced upon you, in other words, that you had to send requests to Mostar each time you wanted to use the military police, how did you actually operate it? Did you actually send your request to Mostar every time, or did you use other ways of work?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I frequently was not in a position to send my requests to Mostar because, let's say in this case, if the communication lines were down, I would have had to send a courier down, and if the road was secure, this courier would send a written request. I sent requests to the 4th Battalion of the military police, either orders or requests, and I was aware that each order which was to be received by the commander of the military police would be sent on to the chief for consideration, and a determination would be made whether to carry it out or not. I did not agree with this proposed model of function of the military police in December, and I was aware of the fact that the chief of staff, chief of the main staff, was also not agreeing with this because he and I had talked right after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the position of the military police towards your request? Did they carry out those requests or did they delay, or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was a selective approach which they took. When it was in their interests, then such a task could be carried out, but when the judgment was that it wasn't convenient for them, then I would often get word that they were waiting for approval from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. What other significant events can you recall of 2nd January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We took additional steps regarding this incident, in other words, to put up a fence around the hotel and to build gates so that we would prevent similar incidents of opening fire at the command post. On that day, we had an additional problem in that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had blocked the road which leads from Travnik to Mehuric where we had a shift which was manning the positions towards the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- army of Republika Srpska. The problem that we had was deployment of Mujahedeen, that is the foreign soldiers, in that village, and according to the information I had, they had fenced off an area for themselves, including a portion of the road, and prevented any traffic along this communication line towards the front line. I also asked of the military police -- and this was an earlier request -- to turn over the checkpoints to the civilian police and to hand over, in other words, to conduct a hand-over, formal hand-over, between the military police and the civilian police of Herceg-Bosna. However, the deadline was not met, and I again asked that this be done. In the course of the day, I learned that the communications with Vares were down, but that was nothing unusual. This was almost a daily occurrence. I also received information about violence in the town of Vitez, opening of fire as an act of provocation by the special purpose unit Vitezovi in the course of the 2nd of January. On that day, we also worked on a draft of a plan of operation in command posts and in the barracks; that is, when, on the 1st of December, when the chief of staff of the Operative Zone started working on the 1st of December, we heard that this would be controlled, that there would be regular controls, and it often happened that when we wanted to go and conduct controls, oftentimes we would not find anyone, and so we wanted to ensure that certain business hours were defined so that people would be in their posts. On that day, I worked on a plan of training of soldiers to use personal weapons. I also asked that the old stamps be discontinued because we had certain problems. The old ones were still being used even though they were taken out of circulation. I also wanted to have an inventory of motor vehicles because these motor vehicles were being used for purposes other than the ones they were meant for. These were the vehicles that were used by the military police, but those were vehicles that for a part were confiscated at checkpoints if they did not have the right documents; in other words, if the permits had expired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the 4th of January.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of January, I already received the first information about the investigation regarding the incident of the attempt on my life in Hotel Vitez, and the military police submitted this information. I worked for the most part of that day with the assistant for logistics in order to put together a full inventory of the weapons and equipment at the disposal of the soldiers in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. The following day, on the 5th of January, I was informed that the military police had confiscated a shipment of uniforms, there were 50 of them, during a routine patrol at a checkpoint, and this shipment was discovered in a shipment of humanitarian aid. Later, Dzemo Merdan asked that this shipment be returned to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that he was aware that there were no proper documents accompanying the shipment but that this was a donation for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of January, you, for the first time, learned of the Vance-Owen Plan, and this Vance-Owen Plan is going to be crucial in the next several months. Can you clarify that a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was called to Mostar, to the representative of the defence department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and the chief of staff of the Croatian Defence Council, and I was told that the Vance-Owen Plan had been signed and that the signatures of the other two sides, that is, the Bosniak Muslims and Serbs, were also expected, and that after this document is signed, the demobilisation of all military recruits would ensue, and the tasks of security will be carried out exclusively by the civilian police. It was also stressed to me that additional steps needed to be taken in order to prevent incidents and other excesses because not everybody was going to be happy with the maps that were going to be signed for Central Bosnia. What I was especially concerned about was the deadline of 45 days within which this mobilisation was to be implemented, the mobilisation of all military recruits, that is, their disarming, and I was aware of the fact that we did not have good organisation, not even the proper documents about the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you doubted that the Lasva Valley could be disarmed within 45 days, especially in light of the fact that you were not able to even arm it properly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I doubted it, not only doubted it, but I was very concerned. I was very concerned with the deadline of 45 days for disarming, and this was something that was particularly stressed to me in the meeting because, like in other areas, people armed themselves in this area, and on top of that, I did not have the basis for demobilisation because this is a very complex task which is regulated and implemented by the state, and the people had already been disarmed by the Yugoslav People's Army and the former Territorial Defence, which was part of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, so that these new weapons, in a short period of time, would have been the third time that somebody was disarming the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, what type of information did you receive in terms of the Vance-Owen Plan? What type of plan was it? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was told briefly that Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to be decentralised, that provinces would be established or, as they were called, cantons, and that in the provinces where Croats lived as the majority, the minority populations or groups would have equal rights, also that there would be no borders between the provinces and that the freedom of movement would be total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told where the Croats would be dominant, in which areas, and the HVO, and on the other hand, where -- now I'm talking about the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia which you commanded.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that it was going to be the Travnik province, but I was told this only after everybody signed on, and also that the third Operative Group in Zepce was going to be subordinated to the 3rd corps in Zenica. I was also told that the plan did not envisage that Kiseljak and Kresevo be part of the Travnik province but will more probably be part of the district of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you went back to Central Bosnia. What happened on 7 January?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Later I held a meeting with the commander of the 107th Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Gradacac. I believe that his last name was Mijacevic. He asked for certain assistance because this was the time of the intense attacks of the Serbian army in Gradacac, which was in the Tuzla region, and, to the extent that we could, we provided such assistance. In the course of the day, I had a meeting with members of the Operative Zone command, and I informed them of the contents of my talk with the representatives of the defence department and the chief of staff and transmitted to them the information that I had regarding the plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina and our pending demobilisation. I stressed that the three majority ethnic groups would be constituent units, and I called for a meeting in Kiseljak and Kresevo in order to inform them as well on this developing situation, that is, the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan and the military duties that were before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, you transported a howitzer. What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: When the joint command was established, they asked that the Travnik defence be reinforced with armaments from the main command, and we had received a 155-millimetre howitzer and a multiple rocket launcher, this is a 120-millimetre multiple rocket launcher, and on that day, on the 8th of January, I received an order from the chief of the main staff to return these artillery pieces to the main staff, and these pieces were transported from Travnik to Mostar. During the day, I also conducted a conversation, this is still the 8th of January, with an officer from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, his name is Jasmin Mesaric, about hiring him for the staff of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and to work on the mobilisation affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jasmin Mesaric is a Bosniak Muslim?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is, but he had good professional experience and was one of the best operations officers we had at the time. The next day, 9th of January, 1993, I requested from the military police to supplement their report on the confiscated motor vehicles because I believed that the information I had received was incomplete. I also received information during the day that the Ante Bruno Busic Regiment had arrived in Travnik, and another unit called Ludvig Pavlovic arrived in Vitez from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Ante Bruno Busic unit and the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, both from Mostar. Could you clarify for the Trial Chamber what type of units these were, who were their commanders, and did you have a similar unit deployed in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These were special purpose units of the "A" type. Their commander was the chief of the defence department, and its profile is similar to the one of the Vitezovi unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you list, within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which units were under the direct command of the chief of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These were two types of units. These were the military police units, which again included certain types of combat units, and the other type was the special purpose units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name some of the special purpose units who were under the direct command of the head of the defence department in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was the Ante Bruno Busic Regiment, Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion, the Vitezovi Battalion, Tvrtko Battalion or, as they were called, the Tvrtkovci, then Apostles, this is what they were called, the Alpha Force. These were the special purpose units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Penal Battalion also part of that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were also part of these special purpose units in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation is a bit unusual. The name of this battalion came from the fact that people who established it had been gaoled previously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These units were under the command of the defence department of Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, they were under the direct command of the head of the defence department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This would be equivalent to the Minister of Defence. This is something that is characteristic for the HVO, and I think we want to clarify that a bit further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in relation to these units, was there also a separate chain of command outside of the regular main staff commander of the operative zone and units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, this is an important point. I think we're going to stop now. General Blaskic, what the Judges are asking for, since you experienced this chronology and are very familiar with it, we're asking that you keep in mind your defence in respect of the indictment. In other words, if it's really important for you to review each day of January, February, or March, well, then do it, but try, over the weekend, to concentrate so that the Judges can focus on what was really essential. That's how you could help us as a witness. Of course, you have a chronology of events, many, many things happened, but some of those things are more important than others for your defence, and that's what you have to try to focus on. I think that we're going to stop at this point, and we will resume on Monday at 2.00. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of February, 1999 at 10.00 a.m. 25
